bivy.name: Lake Constance — the standard base for the South Chute
bivy.capacity: HARD overnight quota of 20 people for the whole basin; roughly five individual sites plus one group site are commonly reported, and parties of seven or more must take the group site
bivy.water: Reliable at the lake itself. Constance Creek, which the climbers' trail follows, runs well early in the season and can be dry by late summer — carry water up rather than assuming you will find it on the climb.
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required and Lake Constance is a NAMED QUOTA AREA. Reserve on Recreation.gov; the 20-person cap makes this one of the scarcest permits in the Olympics. Bear canisters required. Older write-ups describing a free self-issued permit at the trailhead are OUT OF DATE.
bivy.notes: The base camp for essentially every ascent by the standard South Chute, reached by a savage climbers' path that gains roughly 3,300 to 3,400 ft in under two miles of hand-over-hand scrambling above the Dosewallips road. The 20-person ceiling is the real planning constraint — it is a basin, not a campground, and it is full most fine weekends.

bivy.name: Dosewallips road-end camps, staging for the washed-out road
bivy.capacity: Several riverside sites in and around the old drive-in campground at the end of the closed road, plus sites near Dose Forks; rarely full
bivy.water: Reliable — the Dosewallips River
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required for any night inside the park boundary, booked on Recreation.gov. Bear canisters required. Sites on the Forest Service side of the boundary below the park have their own rules, so check which side of the line you intend to sleep on.
bivy.notes: THE ROAD HAS BEEN CLOSED BY A WASHOUT SINCE THE EARLY 2000s, so what used to be a drive-in trailhead is now several miles of road walking — the park's own figure adds about 6.5 miles to the round trip, and other accounts quote over five miles each way to the Lake Constance turn-off, so plan on the longer number. It is the single biggest variable on this side of the range and it rules out a casual car-to-car attempt for most people. Bikes are allowed on the closed road and cut the approach time significantly.

bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required, reserved on Recreation.gov. Bear canisters required, and no fires are permitted at this elevation.

bivy.name: Cutthroat Creek trailhead
bivy.capacity: Large gravel lot, roughly 20-30 vehicles; fills on summer weekends with larch-season hikers
bivy.water: None — no potable water at the trailhead. Cutthroat Creek runs below the lot and needs filtering.
bivy.permit: No camping permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day pass covers parking. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, NOT the national park, so there is no backcountry permit system here at all.
bivy.notes: The lot sits a mile up the forest road from SR 20 and has a vault toilet but no water. Parties climbing the South Buttress or Southeast Buttress routinely sleep here or in a pullout on the road in before a pre-dawn start, though the lot itself is signed for day use and how strictly that is read varies; dispersed camping in the trees along the forest road below is the uncontroversial option. Access is entirely gated by the SR 20 winter closure, and the road has been shut for construction windows in recent seasons, so confirm before driving out.

bivy.name: Cutthroat basin climbers' bivy — SOUTH-SIDE routes only
bivy.capacity: Several scattered one- and two-tent pads in the meadows and among the boulders; no established camp, so parties spread out
bivy.water: A stream runs through the basin and is generally reliable through the climbing season, fed by snow patches under the peak. Late-season flow can thin, so carry capacity for a dry night in a hot September.
bivy.permit: None. Dispersed camping on national forest land needs no permit, no reservation and no quota — the opposite of the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
bivy.notes: SERVES THE SOUTH AND SOUTHEAST ROUTES ONLY. The North Ridge is normally approached from the State Creek side, and this bivy does not help that party at all. From the trailhead a way-path leaves the Cutthroat Lake trail, drops to cross the creek and climbs meadows into the bowl under the south and southeast sides, roughly two hours with a pack. Parties camp here to take a long route in a single push rather than commit to a headlamp descent. Ground is a mix of heather bench and talus and the pads are small, so a large party will be split up. The meadows are thin and the basin sees enough traffic to show it.

bivy.name: Cutthroat Lake basin, outside the quarter-mile closure
bivy.capacity: Limited and regulated — the usable ground is set back from the water, so realistically a handful of small parties
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet stream are dependable all season. Treat or filter.
bivy.permit: No permit needed, but a hard rule applies: NO overnight camping within a quarter mile of Cutthroat Lake. Camp outside that radius and you are legal with no paperwork.
bivy.notes: The lake sits about 1.8 miles in with roughly 500 ft of gain, in the basin under the peak's north and east sides. It is a pleasant place to stage, but the quarter-mile closure exists because the shoreline was being loved to death and it is enforced rather than advisory. For a climb of the south side you gain nothing by coming here — the climbers' path branches off well before the lake — so treat it as a rest-day or bad-weather option rather than a staging camp.

bivy.name: Cutthroat Wall base terrace
bivy.capacity: A small flat area under the cliff; room for one or two parties at most
bivy.water: No water on the terrace itself. Fill in Cutthroat Creek low on the approach and carry it up.
bivy.permit: None — dispersed national forest camping, no permit and no quota.
bivy.notes: The approach leaves the old roadbed a quarter mile from the trailhead at cairns, then climbs left through trees and light brush to a flat bench beneath the west-northwest-facing granite. Most parties do these routes car-to-car in a day, so a bivy here is for a late start or a two-day plan rather than standard practice. The wall faces away from morning sun, which makes an early camp less useful than it looks on the map. The crag is sometimes catalogued under Little Liberty Bell, which is the same approach and the same ground.

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground
bivy.capacity: 27 sites, tents and small RVs
bivy.water: Potable water provided in season, shut off once the campground closes for the year.
bivy.permit: No reservations and no permit — first-come, first-served with a nightly fee. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to camp, only to park at the trailhead.
bivy.notes: The closest developed campground to the Cutthroat Creek trailhead, a short drive east on SR 20 along Early Winters Creek. Because nothing here can be booked, arriving Friday evening in July or August is a gamble and the fallback is dispersed camping on a spur road. The season runs roughly May or June through September or October, entirely dependent on when the highway opens and when snow returns.

bivy.name: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby
bivy.capacity: 46 sites, the largest campground on this stretch of highway
bivy.water: Drinking water spigots in season; vault toilets. Water is turned off at the end of the season while the sites stay usable.
bivy.permit: First-come, first-served, nightly fee, no reservation and no permit required.
bivy.notes: Klipchuck sits about a quarter mile off SR 20 in fir and pine down-valley toward Mazama, low enough to be warm and dry when the passes are still wet. Both are a longer drive to the trailhead than Lone Fir, which is the tradeoff for a better chance of finding a site on a busy weekend.

bivy.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends
bivy.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
bivy.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.

bivy.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots among the larches; the standard base for the north end of the ridge
bivy.water: Present early in the season from snowmelt and the creek drainage, but limited to non-existent by late summer and early autumn. Higher up, a tarn around 7,100 ft and year-round snow at Burgundy Col are the late-season backups.
bivy.permit: None — no reservation, no quota, no backcountry permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle at the pullout below.
bivy.notes: The one genuinely used high camp on the Kangaroo Ridge side, reached by a steep switchbacking climbers' trail that gains roughly 2,000 ft from the highway. It is the sensible base for Vasiliki Ridge and Vasiliki Tower, for the WEST side of Juno Tower, and for linking two or three routes over a weekend rather than re-walking the approach each morning. Juno's east-side routes are a different problem — a 2.5 to 3.5 hour approach with a valley camp in Silver Star Creek — and this camp does not serve them. Bugs can be bad in July; water availability is what actually varies.

bivy.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside parking
bivy.capacity: A moderate paved lot that fills early on weekends; overnight use is vehicle-based only
bivy.water: No potable supply at the trailhead. Blue Lake itself is a mile up the trail and is off limits for camping.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park. No overnight backcountry permit and no reservation — this is national forest, not a North Cascades park camping zone. Overnight camping is prohibited within a quarter mile of Blue Lake.
bivy.notes: Parties climbing the Liberty Bell group frequently sleep here, and it works as a fallback for the Kangaroo Ridge and roadside objectives when the hairpin lot is full, since it is only a few minutes' drive west. Be clear on the distinction: sleeping in the lot is tolerated, but walking up and pitching a tent at the lake is not. There is no water source you can rely on at the parking area.

bivy.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
bivy.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile
bivy.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
bivy.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
bivy.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and several accounts say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. Elevation figures for the pass are not consistently reported, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.

bivy.name: Upper Cedar Creek basin, east of Big Kangaroo
bivy.capacity: Open, rocky basin with room for a few parties on durable ground
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small seasonal pools early; expect nothing dependable once the snow has gone. Carry capacity for a dry camp.
bivy.permit: None required. Still Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest on this side of the divide — no quota permit and no reservation, in contrast to the national park backcountry zones a short distance west.
bivy.notes: Anything on the east side of Kangaroo Ridge is far enough from the road that a bivy makes sense, and the barren upper basin east of Big Kangaroo is the accepted place for it. The usual way in is to follow the Half Moon north-ridge approach from the hairpin and cross the ridge at a low saddle between Half Moon and Big Kangaroo. The ground is stony and almost lunar, which makes it durable but also means no shelter and no vegetation to screen a camp. Reported elevations vary, so plan for a high, cold, waterless site rather than a number.

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds

bivy.name: Sloan Peak high camp — heather benches above Cougar Creek
bivy.capacity: Small, scattered pockets — a few tents on heather and gravel benches; no single site holds a large party
bivy.water: Cougar Creek below the benches and snowmelt runnels near camp are reliable into midsummer; by late August the higher pockets can dry and parties may need to descend or melt snow
bivy.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead box; no reservation or quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group size limited to 12.
bivy.notes: Camps here sit on open heather with the Sloan Glacier and the start of the corkscrew ledge system directly above, which makes for a short summit morning. Lower bivy pockets exist around 3,500 ft where the trail eases off, and some parties stop there when the river ford has eaten the day. EVERYTHING ABOVE THE TRAILHEAD DEPENDS ON THE NORTH FORK SAUK FORD, which is the genuine crux of the trip: it has no bridge, runs fast and thigh-deep or worse in snowmelt, and log jams that worked one season are gone the next. Camp on bare ground or snow rather than the meadow turf, which is thin and slow to recover.

bivy.name: Vesper Creek basin and Lake Elan, beyond Headlee Pass
bivy.capacity: Several tents — grassy benches above the stream just past the pass, plus more spread around the lake basin
bivy.water: Reliable — the basin outlet stream runs all season and the lake itself is a backup, though it holds ice and snow cover well into July
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest but OUTSIDE any wilderness — no permit of any kind to camp. Northwest Forest Pass required at the Sunrise Mine trailhead.
bivy.notes: The working base camp for Vesper Peak's north side and for Sperry, and it puts Morning Star within reach along the ridge. Getting here means the Sunrise Mine trail's ford of the South Fork Stillaguamish, then the switchbacked chute below Headlee Pass at roughly 4,700 ft, which is loose and known for rockfall — parties should not stack up in it. Snow lingers in the chute and on the pass long after the valley is clear, and it is the section most likely to turn an overnight around. Camp on the durable benches rather than the meadow closest to the water. No elevation is recorded; none was confidently sourced.

bivy.name: Foggy Lake, Gothic Basin
bivy.capacity: Moderate — established pockets on the south shore and on the bench toward the base of Gothic; the basin absorbs a fair number of parties but fills on good weekends
bivy.water: The lake is the water source and is dependable, but it is frequently frozen or snow-covered into July, so early-season parties should expect to melt or find running melt below the outlet
bivy.permit: National forest land, NOT wilderness — no camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. Campfires are prohibited in the basin.
bivy.notes: From here both Del Campo and Gothic go as short snow-and-scramble outings, which is why parties carry in rather than push either from the road. The approach leaves Barlow Pass on the old road grade before turning up a steep, rocky climbers' trail with slabby sections that are unpleasant when wet. The basin is bare rock and thin alpine soil with almost nothing to bury waste in, so pack it out. Whether the basin is a July trip or an August one moves year to year with the snowpack.

bivy.name: Monte Cristo townsite, walk-in from Barlow Pass
bivy.capacity: Small — roughly half a dozen developed sites with tables, fire rings and a toilet, plus scattered backcountry spots along the way in
bivy.water: River and creek water nearby, plentiful but untreated — filter or boil
bivy.permit: Outside designated wilderness at the townsite itself; no camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Barlow Pass. The peaks above, including the Columbia Glacier group, sit in the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness where the free self-issue permit applies.
bivy.notes: Reaching it is a flat four-mile walk on the old road and rail grade from the Barlow Pass gate, which makes it an easy place to stage a long approach without a real backpacking day. Climbers use it mainly as a jumping-off point deeper into the Monte Cristo group rather than for Vesper or Sloan. Barlow Pass itself is the usual car-bivy for early starts on Gothic Basin, though it is a parking area rather than a campground — no water, no facilities, and it fills. The site is historic mining ground with old debris and open workings, so wander off the beaten paths carefully.

bivy.name: Bedal Campground, Mountain Loop Highway
bivy.capacity: Around 20 developed sites with tables, tent pads, fire rings and vault toilets; fee campground, typically open late spring to fall
bivy.water: No treated drinking water at the sites — bring your own or filter from the adjacent river
bivy.permit: Developed fee campground on national forest land; the per-night fee covers it and no pass or permit is needed to occupy a site. Nothing here is inside wilderness.
bivy.notes: The closest road camp to the Sloan Peak and Bedal Creek trailheads, and the standard place to sleep the night before a Sloan attempt since the useful start time is well before dawn. It sits on the UNPAVED stretch of the loop, so access depends entirely on whether the seasonal gate between Barlow Pass and the Bedal area is open — the road normally closes around early November and reopens in the second half of May, with the exact date set by snow and washout repairs. Coming from Granite Falls when that gate is shut means the long drive around through Darrington. Check the Darrington district's road status, because the gate has opened as late as Memorial Day in heavy years.

bivy.name: Verlot corridor campgrounds — Turlo, Verlot and Gold Basin
bivy.capacity: Large by the standards of this valley — dozens of developed sites across the three, tables, toilets, some with potable water; fee sites, reservable in part
bivy.water: Verlot and Gold Basin generally have drinking water in season; the Stillaguamish runs alongside as a backup
bivy.permit: Developed fee campgrounds, no permit. None are in wilderness. A Northwest Forest Pass is what you need for the trailheads up the road, not for the sites themselves.
bivy.notes: These sit on the paved lower half of the loop and stay reachable when the gravel section above Barlow Pass is gated shut, which makes them the fallback base for Vesper, Morning Star, Sperry and the Big Four side of the valley. They are closer to the Sunrise Mine and Big Four trailheads than anything up-valley, at the cost of being low, wooded and busy with general campers rather than climbers. Weekend availability is genuinely tight in midsummer, so a reservation is worth having. Dispersed roadside pullouts along the corridor need no permit but are increasingly signed and patrolled.

bivy.water: Verlot and Gold Basin generally have drinking water in season; the Stillaguamish runs alongside as a backup
bivy.permit: Developed fee campgrounds, no permit. None are in wilderness. A Northwest Forest Pass is what you need for the trailheads up the road, not for the sites themselves.
bivy.notes: These sit on the paved lower half of the loop and stay reachable when the gravel section above Barlow Pass is gated shut, which makes them the fallback base for Vesper, Morning Star, Sperry and the Big Four side of the valley. They are closer to the Sunrise Mine and Big Four trailheads than anything up-valley, at the cost of being low, wooded and busy with general campers rather than climbers. Weekend availability is genuinely tight in midsummer, so a reservation is worth having. Dispersed roadside pullouts along the corridor need no permit but are increasingly signed and patrolled.

bivy.name: Sloan Peak high camp — heather benches above Cougar Creek
bivy.capacity: Small, scattered pockets — a few tents on heather and gravel benches; no single site holds a large party
bivy.water: Cougar Creek below the benches and snowmelt runnels near camp are reliable into midsummer; by late August the higher pockets can dry and parties may need to descend or melt snow
bivy.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead box; no reservation or quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group size limited to 12.
bivy.notes: Camps here sit on open heather with the Sloan Glacier and the start of the corkscrew ledge system directly above, which makes for a short summit morning. Lower bivy pockets exist around 3,500 ft where the trail eases off, and some parties stop there when the river ford has eaten the day. EVERYTHING ABOVE THE TRAILHEAD DEPENDS ON THE NORTH FORK SAUK FORD, which is the genuine crux of the trip: it has no bridge, runs fast and thigh-deep or worse in snowmelt, and log jams that worked one season are gone the next. Camp on bare ground or snow rather than the meadow turf, which is thin and slow to recover.

bivy.name: Vesper Creek basin and Lake Elan, beyond Headlee Pass
bivy.capacity: Several tents — grassy benches above the stream just past the pass, plus more spread around the lake basin
bivy.water: Reliable — the basin outlet stream runs all season and the lake itself is a backup, though it holds ice and snow cover well into July
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest but OUTSIDE any wilderness — no permit of any kind to camp. Northwest Forest Pass required at the Sunrise Mine trailhead.
bivy.notes: The working base camp for Vesper Peak's north side and for Sperry, and it puts Morning Star within reach along the ridge. Getting here means the Sunrise Mine trail's ford of the South Fork Stillaguamish, then the switchbacked chute below Headlee Pass at roughly 4,700 ft, which is loose and known for rockfall — parties should not stack up in it. Snow lingers in the chute and on the pass long after the valley is clear, and it is the section most likely to turn an overnight around. Camp on the durable benches rather than the meadow closest to the water. No elevation is recorded; none was confidently sourced.

bivy.name: Foggy Lake, Gothic Basin
bivy.capacity: Moderate — established pockets on the south shore and on the bench toward the base of Gothic; the basin absorbs a fair number of parties but fills on good weekends
bivy.water: The lake is the water source and is dependable, but it is frequently frozen or snow-covered into July, so early-season parties should expect to melt or find running melt below the outlet
bivy.permit: National forest land, NOT wilderness — no camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. Campfires are prohibited in the basin.
bivy.notes: From here both Del Campo and Gothic go as short snow-and-scramble outings, which is why parties carry in rather than push either from the road. The approach leaves Barlow Pass on the old road grade before turning up a steep, rocky climbers' trail with slabby sections that are unpleasant when wet. The basin is bare rock and thin alpine soil with almost nothing to bury waste in, so pack it out. Whether the basin is a July trip or an August one moves year to year with the snowpack.

bivy.name: Monte Cristo townsite, walk-in from Barlow Pass
bivy.capacity: Small — roughly half a dozen developed sites with tables, fire rings and a toilet, plus scattered backcountry spots along the way in
bivy.water: River and creek water nearby, plentiful but untreated — filter or boil
bivy.permit: Outside designated wilderness at the townsite itself; no camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Barlow Pass. The peaks above, including the Columbia Glacier group, sit in the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness where the free self-issue permit applies.
bivy.notes: Reaching it is a flat four-mile walk on the old road and rail grade from the Barlow Pass gate, which makes it an easy place to stage a long approach without a real backpacking day. Climbers use it mainly as a jumping-off point deeper into the Monte Cristo group rather than for Vesper or Sloan. Barlow Pass itself is the usual car-bivy for early starts on Gothic Basin, though it is a parking area rather than a campground — no water, no facilities, and it fills. The site is historic mining ground with old debris and open workings, so wander off the beaten paths carefully.

bivy.name: Bedal Campground, Mountain Loop Highway
bivy.capacity: Around 20 developed sites with tables, tent pads, fire rings and vault toilets; fee campground, typically open late spring to fall
bivy.water: No treated drinking water at the sites — bring your own or filter from the adjacent river
bivy.permit: Developed fee campground on national forest land; the per-night fee covers it and no pass or permit is needed to occupy a site. Nothing here is inside wilderness.
bivy.notes: The closest road camp to the Sloan Peak and Bedal Creek trailheads, and the standard place to sleep the night before a Sloan attempt since the useful start time is well before dawn. It sits on the UNPAVED stretch of the loop, so access depends entirely on whether the seasonal gate between Barlow Pass and the Bedal area is open — the road normally closes around early November and reopens in the second half of May, with the exact date set by snow and washout repairs. Coming from Granite Falls when that gate is shut means the long drive around through Darrington. Check the Darrington district's road status, because the gate has opened as late as Memorial Day in heavy years.

bivy.name: Glacier Meadows — the standard Blue Glacier base camp
bivy.capacity: A cluster of individual sites plus a group site, under a nightly quota; the single most contested permit on this approach
bivy.water: Reliable — meltwater creeks in the meadows; treat it, and expect it to run silty in hot weather
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required, QUOTA-LIMITED, reserved on Recreation.gov. Bear canisters mandatory. Practically every party climbing Olympus wants this camp, so treat the permit as the crux of the trip rather than an afterthought.
bivy.notes: The standard base camp, roughly seventeen miles from the Hoh trailhead and the last established camp before the Blue Glacier — the park does not permit camping between here and the ice. From the meadows you climb the moraine, drop onto the glacier and work up past the Snow Dome to the summit rock, generally quoted as four to six miles and around 3,500 ft of gain each way, so most parties leave in the dark. Sources differ on the elevation, giving anything between about 4,200 and 4,400 ft, which matters only because published gain figures vary with it. A ranger station and pit toilets are here in season.

bivy.name: Elk Lake Camp, Hoh River trail
bivy.capacity: A small handful of individual sites; it fills every summer night in season
bivy.water: Reliable — Elk Lake itself, plus creeks nearby; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required and this is an explicitly quota-limited camp — reserve on Recreation.gov well ahead. Summer-season reservations open in mid-April and the popular Hoh camps can be gone the same morning.

bivy.name: Burgundy Col high camp — WEST side, the Wine Spires
bivy.capacity: Two to four rock-ringed bivy platforms; roughly one is level enough for a two-person tent, so a large party should expect to sleep scattered or send some members back down

The main reason to know about them is that the water situation on this hillside is patchy rather than uniform, so a dry creek at the wooded bench does not necessarily mean a dry mountainside above it. Anyone counting on this should carry a stove and be prepared to find nothing.

bivy.name: Upper Silver Star Creek basin camp — EAST side, Silver Star only
bivy.capacity: Open alpine benches with room for several tents; sites are unimproved and parties spread out
bivy.water: Reliable through the climbing season from the creek and from meltwater draining the glacier, and typically abundant under spring snow — a marked contrast to the col.
bivy.permit: None. Same National Forest, non-wilderness status; no permit and no reservation, though the pullout is still gated by the seasonal highway closure.
bivy.notes: SERVES THE EAST AND NORTH APPROACH up Silver Star Creek, which reaches the glacier near its toe rather than crossing Burgundy Col — it is no use for the Wine Spires on the west side. It is the better choice under spring snow cover, when the drainage skis or snowshoes well and the col approach is a loose, avalanche-prone mess. Later in the summer the same ground turns brushy, and the scree and talus above make it less appealing than the shorter western approach.

bivy.name: Lower Silver Star Creek basin — EAST side, Silver Star only
bivy.capacity: Informal; flat ground on either side of the drainage, several parties
bivy.water: Silver Star Creek runs here through the season, so water is not a planning constraint at this elevation
bivy.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside wilderness; standard dispersed-camping rules apply.
bivy.notes: The drainage levels out near a cascade at about this height, roughly two miles up from the highway, and it is where many parties cross to the west side before continuing. It works as a low, sheltered camp for a ski approach or for a party that started late, but it leaves a long day to the summit. On the east approach it is a waypoint more often than a destination, with most parties pushing on to the upper basin.

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
bivy.capacity: 27 developed first-come, first-served sites for tents and small vehicles
bivy.water: Developed campground with potable water when open; Early Winters Creek runs alongside
bivy.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.
bivy.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.
